en: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa, First Part, First Chapter (Prapāṭhaka)

Om. In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone; it was itself one only. It considered: "I am indeed a great being (yakṣa), yet I am alone. Come now, let me create from myself a second deity who is my very measure. It exerted itself, it heated itself, it brooded over itself. From it—exhausted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon—there came moisture, that which is fluidity, upon its forehead.
He was born; therefore Ānanda said to him: "Truly, we have found a great Yakṣa, well-known.

Because he said, "Truly, we have found a great Yakṣa, well-known," therefore he became Suveda. Although he is this very Suveda, they call him Sveda by an indirect name, for the gods love the indirect as it were, and dislike the direct. — Gopatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1 —

He labored further, he heated himself further, he tormented himself further; from all the pores of his skin, as he was weary, heated, and thoroughly tormented, streams of sweat flowed forth separately.

He rejoiced in them and said: "By these indeed I shall support everything here, whatever exists; by these indeed I shall generate everything here, whatever exists; by these indeed I shall attain everything here, whatever exists."

Because he said, "By these indeed I shall support everything here, whatever exists," therefore they became *dhārās*; that is the *dhārātva* (supporting-nature) of the *dhārās*, since whatever is supported in them [is supported by them].
Because he said, "By these indeed I shall procreate everything here, whatever exists," therefore they became *jāyās*;
that is the *jāyātva* (procreative-nature) of the *jāyās*, since both the man and the son are born (*jāyate*) in them—[the son] from whom one is delivered from the hell named *punnāman*.
Because he saved him from many hundreds [of dangers], the son thus possesses the status of being a son.

As for what he said, "By means of these, indeed, I shall obtain all this, whatever exists," therefore they became the waters; that is the essence of the waters (*aptvam*). He who knows this obtains all desires whatsoever he may desire.
Having created those waters, he gazed upon them; while he was gazing at his own reflection in them, his semen spontaneously fell.

That [water] established itself in the waters; he exerted himself, heated, and brooded over them right there. When they were exhausted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon, they became divided along with the semen. Of those, some were excessively salty, undrinkable, and tasteless; being unappeased, they remained covering the ocean of semen. Then the others were drinkable, sweet, and appeased.

He exerted himself, heated, and brooded over them right there. From them—exhausted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon—that seed which was produced was parched. Because it was parched (*abhṛjyata*), from that Bhṛgu came into being. That is why Bhṛgu’s name is "Bhṛgu.
Indeed, like Bhṛgu, he who knows this shines in all the worlds.

Having created Bhṛgu, he disappeared. That created Bhṛgu moved toward the east; Speech spoke after him, saying, "O Vāyu! O Vāyu! He turned back. He moved toward the southern direction; Speech spoke after him, saying, "O Mātariśvan! O Mātariśvan! He turned back. He moved toward the western direction; Speech spoke after him, saying, "O Pavamāna! O Pavamāna!"

He turned back and moved toward the northern direction; Speech called out after him, "O Wind, blow! He said to her, "Have we not already found him? She replied, "No. "Then seek him again within these very waters," she said. Because she said, "Then seek him again within these very waters," he became Atharvan; that is the origin of Atharvan's name.

Now, indeed, of this venerable seer Atharvan, his entire self came into being just as the hair on the body of Brahmā, just as his limbs, and just as his vital breaths. Having created the creatures of Prajāpati, Brahmā said to that Atharvan: "Protect them!"
Because he said, "Having created the offspring of Prajāpati, protect them," he therefore became Prajāpati;
that is the nature of Prajāpati. Atharvan is indeed Prajāpati. He who knows this shines like Prajāpati in all the worlds.

He exerted himself toward that seer Atharvan, he heated him, he brooded over him; from him, thus exerted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon, he fashioned forth the ten-fold Atharvan seers: those consisting of one verse, two verses, three verses, four verses, five verses, six verses, seven verses, eight verses, nine verses, and ten verses.

He exerted himself toward those Atharvan seers; he heated them, he intensely brooded over them. From them—exhausted, heated, and intensely brooded upon—he fashioned the ten-fold Atharvanic lineages: the eleven-fold, the twelve-fold, the thirteen-fold, the fourteen-fold, the fifteen-fold, the sixteen-fold, the seventeen-fold, the eighteen-fold, the nineteen-fold, and the twenty-fold.
He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those seers of the Atharvans and the lineages of the Atharvans;
from them—exhausted, heated, and intensely heated—the mantras which he beheld became the Atharva Veda.
He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated that Atharva Veda; from it—exhausted, heated, and intensely heated—[the mantras emerged].

"Om"—the syllable *om* alone ascended upward as the highest syllable. If one should desire, "May I perform [this rite] with all these Atharvans and Atharvaṇic hymns," he should perform it with this very Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
For him who knows thus, and for him who, knowing thus, performs it with this Great Utterance, it becomes performed with all these Atharvans and Atharvaṇic hymns. (Gopatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.5)
He labored further, he heated himself further, he tormented himself further. From his very self, he fashioned the three worlds: the earth, the intermediate space, and the sky.
Indeed, from his two feet he fashioned the earth, from his belly the intermediate space, and from his head the sky.
He labored over those three worlds, he heated them, he tormented them; from them—being thus labored, heated, and tormented—he fashioned the three deities: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya.

He indeed fashioned fire from the earth, wind from the intermediate space, and the sun from the sky. He exerted himself toward, brooded over, and intensely heated those three deities; from them, thus exerted, brooded upon, and intensely heated, he fashioned the three Vedas—the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda—[specifically] the Ṛgveda from Agni.

From Vāyu he drew forth the Yajurveda, and from Āditya the Sāmaveda. He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those three Vedas; from them, thus exerted, brooded upon, and intensely heated, he fashioned the three Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti): Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
"Bhūḥ" from the Ṛgveda, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajurveda, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāmaveda.
If one should desire, "May I perform [this rite] with all these three Vedas," he should perform it with these very Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis).
For him who knows thus, and for whosoever else [knows thus], this rite becomes performed by means of all these three Vedas.
The wise man thus performs [the rites] with these great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis).
Those waters which, having encompassed the ocean, stood there, flowed together toward the east, south, west, and north.
Because they flowed together (*samavadravanta*), it is therefore called the ocean (*samudra*).
Terrified, they said, "We choose the Blessed One himself as our king."

And because he stood having chosen [it], he became Varuṇa; though being that very Varuṇa, they call him Varuṇa cryptically, for the gods, as it were, prefer the cryptic and dislike the manifest. He was released from the ocean; he became Mucyu; though being that very Mucyu, they call him Mṛtyu.

For the gods, as it were, prefer what is out of sight; they dislike what is manifest. He exerted himself toward, brooded over, and intensely heated that Varuṇa, who is Death. From all his limbs, as he was thus exhausted, brooded upon, and intensely heated, the essence flowed forth; that became the Aṅgarasa (the "limb-essence"). Indeed, him being that very Aṅgarasa—
They call him Aṅgiras;
for the gods love the cryptic, as it were, and dislike the manifest.

He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated that seer Aṅgiras; from him, thus exerted, brooded over, and intensely heated, he fashioned forth the twenty Aṅgiras seers. He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those twenty Aṅgiras seers; from them, thus exerted, brooded over, and intensely heated, [he fashioned] the tenfold lineages of the Aṅgiras seers.

He fashioned the *ṣoḍaśins*, the *aṣṭādaśins*, the *dvādaśins*, those consisting of one verse, three verses, four verses, five verses, six verses, two verses, and seven verses. He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those seers, the Aṅgirases, and the lineages of the Aṅgirases; from them, thus exhausted...

From those [sages] who were heated and thoroughly scorched, the mantras which he, the descendant of Aṅgiras, perceived became the Veda. He exerted himself over that Veda of the Aṅgirases, he brooded over it, he intensely heated it; from it, being thus exerted, heated, and thoroughly scorched, the two-syllabled word "janad" emerged.
If one should desire, "May I perform [this] with all these Aṅgirases and descendants of Aṅgiras," he should perform it with this very Great Utterance (mahāvyāhṛti).
Verily, for him who knows thus, and who, being wise, performs it in this way with this Great Utterance, it becomes performed by all these Aṅgirases and descendants of Aṅgiras.
He stood upright; he propped apart these worlds. Therefore, an Aṅgiras who studies stands upright;
that is his vow. He should meditate with his mind: "Whatever I shall meditate upon with my mind, even that shall come to pass.
And indeed, it came to pass exactly so.
This has also been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:

"The Veda, born from austerity, is indeed the best; it came into being for the destruction of those who violate the Brahman. That which was created as the straight-moving reality, this dwelling—'May he be far from debt'.
These very *menis* are the sisters of the Aṅgirases; he who knows this performs his work with the *menis* and attains heroic power.

He looked toward the quarters: the east, the south, the west, the north, the fixed zenith, and the upward direction. He exerted himself, heated, and thoroughly brooded over them; from them, thus exerted, heated, and thoroughly brooded over, he fashioned forth five Vedas: the Serpent Veda, the Piśāca Veda, the Asura Veda, the Itihāsa Veda, and the Purāṇa Veda.

From the eastern direction, he indeed fashioned the Sarpaveda; from the southern, the Piśācaveda; from the western, the Asuraveda; from the northern, the Itihāsaveda; and from the fixed and the upward directions, the Purāṇaveda.

He exerted himself over, brooded over, and intensely heated those five Vedas; from them, when they were thus exerted, brooded upon, and intensely heated, he fashioned the five great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*): *vṛdhat*, *karat*, *guhat*, *mahat*, and *tat*.
"Vṛdhat" from the Sarpaveda; "karat" from the Piśācaveda; "guhāt" from the Asuraveda; "mahat" from the Itihāsaveda;

and "tat" from the Purāṇaveda. If one should desire, "May I perform [the sacrifice] with all these five Vedas," he should perform it with these very Mahāvyāhṛtis; for indeed, by this, his performance is accomplished through all these five Vedas.
Whoever knows thus, and whoever, knowing thus, performs [the rites] with these great utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis).

He looked toward both the near and the distant; he exerted himself, heated, and brooded over them right there. From them—exhausted, heated, and thoroughly brooded upon—the syllable *śam* emerged upward.
If one should desire, "May I perform [this] with all these near and distant [syllables]," he should do so by means of this very [syllable].

One should perform [the rite] with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti). Indeed, for one who knows thus, and for one who, knowing thus, performs it with this Great Utterance, everything becomes accomplished by means of all these [utterances], both those that are near and those that are far. GpBr 1.1.11.

He labored further, he heated himself further, he disciplined himself further. From his mind alone he fashioned the moon; from his nails the stars, from his body hair the plants and trees, and from his minor vital breaths many other gods. He labored further, he heated himself further, he disciplined himself further. He beheld this sacrifice, which is threefold, seven-threaded, and culminates in twenty-one parts.
This is also stated in a Rigvedic verse:
"Agni [performs] the seven-threaded, threefold sacrifice.
Furthermore, this well-known traditional verse declares: "There are seven Soma sacrifices and seven Pākayajñas."

He brought that [sacrifice] with which he sacrificed; Agni was its *hotṛ*, Vāyu its *adhvaryu*, Sūrya its *udgātṛ*, Candramas its *brahmán*, Parjanya its *sadasya*, the plants and trees were the *camasādhvaryus*, the Viśvedevas were the *hotraka*s, and the Atharvans and Aṅgirases were the protectors.
Those ancient scholars learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*s), knowing this, having concluded the sacrifice, used to say: "So be it! (or, "It is accomplished!").

"Let this sacrificial vessel (gharma) not overtake us while we are negligent; O immortals, let it not consume our offspring!"—thus they say of those who run forward as protectors, the attendants of the assembly hall (*sadas*), who are enriched by the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Regarding this, Prajāpati indeed said: "When the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at the sacrifice are unskilled, lacking in practice, and have failed in their celibacy (*brahmacarya*),"
Or rather, they say that this is indeed a fracture of the sacrifice.
Following the fracture of the sacrifice, the sacrificer is fractured; following the fracture of the sacrificer, the officiating priests are fractured;
following the fracture of the officiating priests, the sacrificial fees are fractured; and following the fracture of the sacrificial fees, the sacrificer is fractured in his sons and cattle.

"He is deprived of his sons and cattle; following the deprivation of the sacrificer, he is deprived of the heavenly world; following the deprivation of the heavenly world, the security and prosperity (yogakṣema) of that half [of the world] is deprived in which half they sacrifice," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
If those who have failed in a sacrifice, or those whose sacrifice has been damaged, should approach such a Brahmin who knows this [rite],

saying, "Homage be to you, O Blessed One! Please mend for us what is damaged in our sacrifice," then, wherever the damage may be, he should kindle the fires, prepare water for pacification, and sprinkle the fires three times with the formula, "For the ear of the Earth."

He sprinkles water around [the fire] three times; he causes the one being consecrated to sip water three times, and he sprinkles [him] thoroughly, as well as the sacrificial site. Furthermore, by means of the essence of the Vedas, whatever part of the sacrifice has been injured is joined together. It is just as if one were to join gold with salt, silver with gold, iron with silver, lead with iron, and tin with lead—in this very way, whatever part of his sacrifice has been injured is restored.
Following the joining of the sacrifice, the sacrificer is joined;
following the joining of the sacrificer, the officiating priests are joined; following the joining of the officiating priests, the sacrificial gifts are joined;
following the joining of the sacrificial gifts, the sacrificer is joined with sons and cattle; following the joining of sons and cattle, the sacrificer is joined with the heavenly world.

"One is united with the world of heaven through the union [of the sacrifice]; following that union, the security and prosperity (yogakṣema) of that half [of the world] is secured, in which half they sacrifice—so says the Brāhmaṇa."
Regarding this, Atharvan the god, knowing it, said: "Those who understand the injuries to the sacrifice should pacify the resulting misfortunes; thus an expiation is performed for the sacrifice.

Moreover, even if much that is contrary to the ritual order is done in the sacrifice, no affliction whatsoever shall befall him, nor does he encounter an obstacle to the sacrifice. He strikes down death again, he overcomes rebirth again, and there is freedom of movement."

"He shines in all worlds who knows this; and he who, knowing thus, becomes the Brahman priest; and he for whom a Brahman priest, knowing thus, sits to the south of the sacrificial hall; and he for whom a Brahman priest, knowing thus, sitting to the south facing north, offers the oblations of clarified butter in the sacrifice"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Brahmā indeed created Brahmā at Puṣkara; and that Brahmā, once created, fell into reflection: "By which single syllable might I [attain] all desires, all worlds, all gods, all Vedas, all sacrifices, all sounds, all manifestations, and all beings, both stationary and moving?"

Thinking, "May I experience this," he practiced celibacy; he beheld this syllable *oṃ*, which consists of two letters and four measures, which is all-pervading, all-encompassing, and the undecaying Brahman—the *brāhmī* utterance, having Brahman as its deity. By means of it, [he attained] all desires, all worlds, all gods, all Vedas, and all sacrifices.
He experienced all sounds, all prosperities, and all beings, both stationary and moving;
by its first color he experienced moisture in the waters, and by its second color he experienced heat and the luminaries.

By its first measure of tone, he pervaded the earth, Agni, the herbs and trees, the Rigveda, the Vyāhṛti "bhūḥ," the Gāyatrī metre, the Trivṛt Stoma, the eastern quarter, the spring season, speech, and with respect to the self, the tongue and taste— thus he pervaded these organs.
By its second measure of tone, he attained the intermediate space, the wind, the Yajurveda, the *vyāhṛti* "bhuvaḥ," the *triṣṭubh* metre,
the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa-stoma*), the western quarter, the summer season, the breath within the self, and the sense of smell in the nostrils— thus he attained these organs.
By its third measure of tone, he pervaded the sky, the sun, the Sāmaveda, the *svaḥ* vyāhṛti, the Jāgata metre,
the seventeenfold Stoma, the northern quarter, the rainy season, light, the eye with respect to the self, and sight— thus the sense organs.
By means of the mere syllable *va*, he experienced the waters, the moon, the Atharvaveda, the stars, the sound *oṃ*, his own self, the people,

the *ānuṣṭubh* metre of the Aṅgirases, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), the southern quarter, the autumn season, the mind as the internal organ, knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the senses. Thus he pervaded them.
By the sound of the syllable *makāra*, he experienced the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, the Vāka, the Vākyas, the Gāthās, the Nārāśaṃsīs, the Upaniṣads, and the Anuśāsanās;
the Vyāhṛtis beginning with *vṛdhat*, *karat*, *guhant*, *mahat*, *tat*, *śam*, and *oṃ*; the various strings of the lute; vocal music, dance, song, and instrumental music;
the Caitraratha deity; the lightning-light; the Vārhat Sāman; the Tṛṇavat metre; and the two Triṣṭubhs of thirty-three syllables.

The two *stoma*s, the fixed upward direction, the two seasons of winter and cool weather, and the sense of hearing within the self— the perception of sound— thus he experienced as the organs of sense.

This very syllable, the *ṛc*, appeared in the beginning from the austerity of Brahmā; it is the pure *Atharva-veda* of the Veda. From that very source the mantras appeared. Now, whatever in the mantras one makes deficient, defective, or exhausted through lack of austerity, lack of service, or by reciting on forbidden days (*anadhyāya*), that the mantras of the Atharvans restore and replenish through their splendor.
And so that they may turn toward me, like embryos seeking to reach their mother, one should employ the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning;
with this very verse one should cause them to swell again. This [verse] is employed at the front of the sacrifice, this one at the back; by means of this, the sacrifice is extended on all sides.
This has also been stated in a Rigvedic verse:

"That which is joined in the east, in the syllable, in the highest heaven. A Brahmin who desires whatever wish he may have, having fasted for three nights, facing eastward and restraining his speech, [should recite it] upon the sacrificial grass.
"Having sat down, one should repeat it a thousand times; thus his purposes and all his rites are accomplished," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
The Asuras surrounded that city of Indra, which was a continuous stream of *vasordhārā* offerings; those gods became afraid, wondering, "Who will slay these Asuras?
They beheld Oṃkāra, the eldest son of Brahmā, and they said to him, "May we conquer these Asuras with you as our mouth."
He said, "What will be my reward? [The other] said, "Choose a boon. "I choose," he replied, and he chose this boon:
"May the Brahmins not speak of the *brahman* without having sent for me; if they should speak it, let that be no *brahman*. "So be it," [they said].
Those gods were engaged in conflict with the Asuras on the northern part of the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*). From the *agnīdhrīya* fire, the gods [addressed] them with the syllable *oṃ*.
They overpowered the Asuras; because they overpowered them, therefore the syllable *oṃ* is uttered first.
Indeed, he who does not know this *oṃkāra* would be without mastery; but he who knows it becomes a master of Brahman.
Therefore, the *oṃkāra* is the *ṛc* in the *ṛgveda*, the *yajus* in the *yajurveda*, the *sāman* in the *sāmaveda*, the *sūtra* in the *sūtras*, and the *brāhmaṇa* in the *brāhmaṇas*.
"Verse upon verse, the syllable *praṇava* upon the syllable *praṇava*"—this is the Brāhmaṇa.

We ask about the syllable *oṃ*: what is its root (*dhātu*), what is its nominal stem (*prātipadika*), what is its noun (*nāman*) or verb (*ākhyāta*), what is its gender (*liṅga*), what is its number (*vacana*), what is its case (*vibhakti*), what is its suffix (*pratyaya*), what is its accent (*svara*), is it a prefix (*upasarga*) or a particle (*nipāta*), what indeed is its grammar (*vyākaraṇa*),

what is its modification (*vikāra*), what is the modified base (*vikārī*), how many morae (*mātrā*) does it have, how many phonemes (*varṇa*) does it have, how many syllables (*akṣara*) does it have, how many words (*pada*) does it have, what is its conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and what are its place of articulation (*sthāna*), effort (*anupradāna*), and instrument (*karaṇa*)?

"What do students recite? What is the metre? What is the phoneme?"—these are the preliminary questions. Then follow the subsequent ones: "What is the mantra? What is the ritual manual (kalpa)? What is the explanatory passage (brāhmaṇa)? What are the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman [Vedas]? Why do those who discourse on Brahman (brahmavādinaḥ) place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning? What is its deity? What is its light? What is its etymology (nirukta)? What is its location? What is its material cause (prakṛti)? What is its inner self (adhyātma)?"—these are the thirty-six questions.
The first three groups of twelve [verses] among those preceding and following shall explain the syllable Oṃ for us.

Indra asked Prajāpati: "O Blessed One, having approached you, I ask you a question. "Ask, my son," he replied. "What is this syllable *oṃ*? Whose son is it? What is its meter (*chandas*)? What is its phoneme (*varṇa*)? And how does one become Brahman through this Brahman? Therefore, indeed, he first took hold of that auspicious *oṃkāra*; the *oṃkāra* consists of a single syllable, with the circumflex (*svarita*) and acute (*udātta*) accents.

In the Ṛgveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is acutely accented (*udātta*) with the threefold tone (*traisvarya*). In the Yajurveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is acutely accented with the long and protracted vowels.

In the Sāmaveda, the single-syllable *oṃ* is acutely accented with short vowels. In the Atharvaveda, it consists of two syllables—*a* and *u*—with the acute accent, comprising three and a half morae (*mātrā*), while the letter *m* is said to be the consonant. They say that the first of these morae has Brahmā as its deity and is red in color.

He who constantly meditates upon that [first] measure, which has Brahmā as its deity and is white in color, shall go to the state of Brahmā. That which is the second measure, having Viṣṇu as its deity and black in color—he who constantly meditates upon it shall go to the state of Viṣṇu. That which is the third measure, having Īśāna as its deity and tawny in color—he who constantly meditates upon it shall go to the state of Īśāna. And that which is the three-and-a-halfth...

The Mātrā, belonging to all the deities, having become manifest, moves through the ether like pure crystal; he who meditates constantly upon her by means of that color shall go to the nameless state. Furthermore, that Brahmin who does not know the origin of the syllable Oṃ must undergo the initiation ceremony again; therefore, the word of a Brahmin is to be respected, just as Lātavya was of the Gotra of Brahmā.
The son is the Gāyatrī metre, the white color; the male calf is the deity Rudra, the syllable Om of the Vedas.
"What is the root? [The answer is] the root *āp*. Some also say it is the root *av*, because of the similarity of form; however, the similarity of meaning is closer.

Therefore, from the root *āp* comes the syllable *oṃ*; its meaning is "it attains everything. A nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in a primary suffix (*kṛt*) is meaningful; when there is the non-appearance of a suffix, it becomes a name (*nāman*). And among the particles (*nipāta*), grammarians record this as having the acute accent (*udātta*); thus it is an indeclinable compound (*avyayībhūta*).
"A word that expresses its meaning according to its etymology never changes.
That which remains the same across the three genders, all case endings, and all numbers— that which does not change is called *avyaya* (an indeclinable).

Which [part] undergoes modification? The *prasāraṇa* (vowelization), the *āpti* (attainment), and the *atirāva* (prolongation) up to the vowel *ā*. Which [parts] are modified? The initial *oṃkāra* is modified; the second part, the syllable *ma*, is indeed modified. How many letters and how many syllables does it have? It has two letters and one syllable: *oṃ*. Thus the *oṃkāra* is established. How many morae (*mātrā*) does it have? It has three morae at the beginning, for it floats over [the first three]; the syllable *ma* [occupies] the fourth. What is its place of articulation (*sthāna*)?

Both lips are the place of articulation, and the *nāda* (nasal resonance) and *anupradāna* (effort) are the means of production. A diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*) has two places of articulation, with a trace of the vowel *a*.

The gutturals are as previously stated; the remaining [consonants] are either produced with the organs wide open (*vivṛtakaraṇa*) or with the organs in contact (*spṛṣṭakaraṇa*). There is no conjunction [of consonants] except for *vidyut*. Regarding the verb endings, prefixes, unaccented vowels, circumflex accents, genders, case-endings, and numbers, the teachers of old who studied the *Saṃsthāna* [text] understood them from hearing alone; they did not ask for the underlying cause. Now, as for those belonging to the later school (*aparapakṣīya*):

The poet Pañcālacaṇḍa became an inquirer, saying, "May you each speak of the defects of the *udgītha*. He would then observe that [the chant] according to its phonemes, syllables, words, and accents, and according to the inflection used by the seers; thus they praise speech. For that reason, we say that this [defect] of the phonemes will result in this [consequence]; those who know the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅgavidas) have studied it accordingly.
What is *chandas*? For *chandas* is the *gāyatrī*; indeed, the *gāyatrī* among the gods is explained as having one syllable and being white in color.

There are two groups of twelve [syllables each]; this is the *vyākaraṇa*, which consists of the statement of verbal roots (*dhātu*), the statement of phonetics (*śaikṣya*), and the statement of meters (*chandas*).
Furthermore, the two subsequent groups of twelve are explained as the secret portion of the Veda (*vedarahasyikī*), namely: the *mantra*, the *kalpa*, and the *brāhmaṇa*.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva [Vedas]—these are the Vyahṛtis of the four Vedas in their proper order: "Oṃ," "Bhūḥ," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ" are the Vyahṛtis.

It is heard that at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, the utterances of the sages began to flow forth without due consideration. At this point, the Lord of Faults (Dvaipāyana) fell into anxiety, thinking:

"Soma must be drunk by three [Vedas]; it has become as if incomplete. Consequently, the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas lost their splendor. Thereupon, the great seers lamented: "We have fallen into great grief and fear; yet this [incompleteness] was not brought about by all [of us]."
"We have been instructed by you; we shall all take refuge in the Blessed One alone so that you may be the source of happiness for us all.
Having said, "So be it," they remained silent. [The teacher thought,] "Knowledge is not for those who do not approach; therefore, let them approach. Thus, they humbled themselves and drew near.
He initiated them and said to them, "From the very beginning, you must utter my own *vyāhṛti*s; in this way, my fires are established."

"Soma must not be drunk by those who do not know the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras hymns, O officiating priests; [otherwise] they will perish, the sacrificer will be obscured by passion, and the sacred revelation (Śruti) will remain obscured. In this very way, through each successive application, you shall govern offspring after offspring;
thus your majesty will not suffer defeat. "So be it, so be it, O Blessed One," they accepted, and they caused [him] to swell with strength.
They thus became free from sorrow and fear;
therefore, those who discourse on Brahman place the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning.

"What is its deity? "Agni is the deity of the *ṛc*s; that indeed is the light. The *gāyatrī* is the meter, and the earth is the location. Beginning with the words, "I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the god of the sacrifice, the officiating priest, the invoker, the best bestower of jewels," they study the *Ṛgveda*.

Vāyu is the deity of the *yajus* formulas; that very light is their [deity], the *triṣṭubh* is their meter, and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is their location. Having begun with "For sapidity thee! For vigor thee! O Vāyus, you are [the winds]! May the divine Savitṛ impel you for the most excellent rite," and so forth, they study the *Yajurveda*.
The Ādityas are the deity of the *sāmans*; their light is that very same [light]; the *jagatī* is the metre; and heaven is their station.
Beginning with "O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation;
sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacrificial grass," they study the Sāmaveda.
For the Atharvans, the moon is the deity; that indeed is their light; all the meters are their [deities]; and water is their abode.
Beginning with the verse "May the gods be gracious to us," they study the Atharvaveda.
From water, the entire host of beings, both stationary and moving, comes into existence; therefore, every being consists of water, and everything consists of the Bhrigus and Aṅgirases.

"The three Vedas depart; they take refuge with the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases. Thus, because "Ap" is the source of the waters and because of the syllable *Oṃ*, Vyāsa declared this previously: one who has been consecrated by a knower of the Bhṛgvaṅgirases may study other Vedas, but one not so consecrated shall not study the Bhṛgvaṅgirases. Furthermore, there is a scriptural passage in the *Khila* of the Sāmaveda: "And from this [study] through celibacy comes the Atharvāṅgirasa, which is indeed the Veda."
"He knows everything"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

The syllable *oṃ* is the internal medicine for the self, the absolute liberation of the self; having restrained the self, one should contemplate the thought of the true reality (*bhūtārtha*) beyond all association.

The meaning is that by transcending the Vedas, one attains the supreme fruit of the inner self. Having reflected upon the word according to its true meaning through these questions and answers concerning knowledge accompanied by discursive reasoning (*savitarka*), one becomes a knower of the context.
"For the subject is indeed powerful; 'in every sentence it is the sentence [that prevails],' so says the Brāhmaṇa."

Now, it is said that Glāva Maitreya once approached the eleven-eyed Maudgalya, who was learned in this [knowledge]. While Maudgalya was dwelling with him in studentship (*brahmacarya*), he recognized him and said: "What indeed does this young man recite, that he dwells here in studentship? A pupil of Maudgalya heard this, and having gone to his teacher, he reported it to him.

"He has spoken to you, sir, who are poorly learned, saying, 'What does this guest of today know, gentle sir? He replied, 'The three Vedas, sir. Then he said, 'Gentle sir, let that clear-minded and ambitious pupil of his call for me,' and he summoned him. When he had been summoned, [the teacher] addressed him: 'He there, sir—what does your teacher study? 'The three Vedas.'"

He said, "O, sir! Since we have indeed learned all the Vedas by heart, why does our teacher speak thus? How could the learned ever speak in such a manner to those who are themselves learned? For regarding this question which I ask him, he neither wishes to answer it nor has he studied it."
Maudgalya said to his own pupil: "Go, my dear, approach Glāva Maitreya and study [with him].

My dear, he shall teach you the Sāvitrī—the Gāyatrī with twenty-four origins and twelve pairs, whose eye is the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, and upon which all this is supported. "If, my dear, he proves difficult to study under," [he continued].

The teacher said: "One says that a student recites the Sāvitrī to another student; you shall declare the truth of that. You have indeed spoken ill of Maudgalya regarding his study; as for the question he asked you, you did not answer it.
Before a year has passed, you shall meet with misfortune."

He went to where the other was; he questioned him, but he did not understand it. He said to him, "You have called Maudgalya 'one who studies poorly. As for the question he asked you, you did not answer it; before a year has passed, you shall meet with misfortune."

Then Maitreya said to his own pupils, "Gentlemen, disperse as you please, according to your purpose, your homes, and your inclinations. I spoke harshly to Maudgalya; he asked me a question that I did not answer.
I shall go to him and make peace."

In the morning, Maitreya, with fuel in his hand, approached Maudgalya. "Ho, Maitreya! Why have you come? "I said to you, 'You are not studying well,' because you did not answer the question I asked you;
I am coming to you so that I may bring peace. He replied, "In this matter, indeed, everything has been understood."

"You have wronged me by driving away with this vehicle while you were traveling; this auspicious chariot of mine is yours—I give it to you, so go with it. He replied, "In this very matter, there is brilliance and benevolence, just as you say; I shall come to you. He went to him, and having approached him, he asked: "What indeed do they call the most excellent splendor (*bhargas*) of Savitṛ?"
"What do the sages say regarding the god? Discern the thoughts, if they shall impel him as he goes forth with them.

To him he spoke this: "The Vedas, the meters, and the desirable splendor of the god Savitṛ—the sages call these his food; the ritual acts are the thoughts. This I tell you: those [thoughts] by which Savitṛ impels him as he goes forth."
Having approached him, he asked: "Sir, please teach me: who is Savitṛ, and what is Sāvitrī?"

The mind alone is Savitṛ, and speech is Sāvitrī; for wherever there is mind, there is speech, and wherever there is speech, there is mind—these two are two wombs, a single couple. Agni alone is Savitṛ, and the earth is Sāvitrī; for wherever there is Agni, there is the earth, and wherever there is the earth, there is Agni—these two are two wombs, a single couple. Vāyu alone is Savitṛ, and the intermediate space...
For where there is Vāyu, that is the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and where there is the intermediate space, that is Vāyu; these two are two wombs, a single couple.

Āditya indeed is Savitṛ, and the sky is Sāvitrī; for where there is Āditya, that is the sky, and where there is the sky, that is Āditya; these two are two wombs, a single couple. Candramas indeed is Savitṛ, and the constellations are Sāvitrī.

For where there is Sāvitrī, there indeed are the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and where there are the lunar mansions, there indeed is the moon; these two are two wombs, a single couple. Savitṛ is the day, and Sāvitrī is the night; for where there is the day, there is the night, and where there is the night, there is the day; these two are two wombs, a single couple. Savitṛ is heat, and Sāvitrī is cold.

For where there is heat, that is cold; and where there is cold, that is heat—these two are two wombs, one couple. The cloud is indeed Savitṛ, and the rain is Sāvitrī; for where there is a cloud, there is rain, and where there is rain, there is a cloud—these two are two wombs, one couple. Lightning is indeed Savitṛ, and thunder is Sāvitrī; where...

The lightning is indeed this [light], and the thunder is that; where there is thunder, there is lightning—these two are two wombs, one couple. The breath is Savitṛ, and food is Sāvitrī; for where there is breath, there is food, and where there is food, there is breath—these two are two wombs, one couple. The Vedas are indeed Savitṛ, and the meters are Sāvitrī; where [the Vedas are],...
The Vedas are indeed those meters; where there are meters, there are the Vedas—these two are two wombs, a single couple.

The sacrifice is Savitṛ, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is Sāvitrī; for where there is a sacrifice, there is the sacrificial fee, and where there is the sacrificial fee, there is the sacrifice—these two are two wombs, a single couple. Indeed, this [knowledge] was known by Opākārimāsa, who was swift.

"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) has been established for you"—having said this, he sat down; he became as if piled up like a funeral mound. Then, rising up, he departed as a wandering mendicant. Brahman looked toward this glory, the foundation, the abode; he thought, "Let it perform austerity so that it may be maintained in the vow. It became established in truth. Having created the Brāhmaṇa by means of the Sāvitrī, Savitṛ assigned the Sāvitrī to him.
"That choice-worthy splendor of Savitṛ"—this is the first quarter of the Sāvitrī. He joined the *ṛc* with the earth, and Agni with the *ṛc*.
Through fire one obtains glory; through glory, a wife; through a wife, a couple; through a couple, offspring; through offspring, ritual action;
through ritual action, austerity; through austerity, truth; through truth, the Veda; through the Veda, the Brahmin; through the Brahmin, the vow.
Indeed, by means of the vow, the Brahmin becomes sharpened, he becomes not empty, he becomes uninterrupted; his lineage remains uninterrupted.
The life and existence of one who knows this becomes uninterrupted; and also of one who, knowing thus, explains this first quarter of the Sāvitrī in this manner.
With the second foot of the Sāvitrī, "We meditate upon the splendor of the god," he joined the Yajus with the intermediate space;
with the Yajus, Vāyu; with Vāyu, the cloud; with the cloud, rain; with rain, plants and trees; with plants and trees, animals;
with animals, ritual action; with ritual action, austerity; with austerity, truth; with truth, the Brahman; and with the Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa.
By means of one vow, the Brahmin indeed becomes sharpened through the other; he becomes non-empty, he becomes uninterrupted.
His lineage remains uninterrupted, and his life becomes uninterrupted, for him who knows this, and for him who, knowing thus, explains this second foot of the Sāvitrī in this manner.
With the third foot of the Sāvitrī, "May he impel our thoughts," the Day joined with the *sāman*;
from the *sāman*, the Sun; from the Sun, the rays; by the rays, rain; by rain, the plants and trees;
by the plants and trees, the animals; by the animals, action; by action, austerity; by austerity, truth; by truth, the *brahman*; by the *brahman*, the Brahmin; by the Brahmin, [the Veda].

By means of one vow, the Brahmin indeed becomes sharpened through the vow; he becomes not empty, he becomes uninterrupted. His lineage remains uninterrupted, his life becomes uninterrupted—he who knows this, and he who, knowing thus, explains this third foot of the Sāvitrī in this manner.

Thus, by a Brahmin who knows this, the Brahman is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped; by the Brahman, space is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped; by space, air is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped; by air, light is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped; by light, water is pervaded, swallowed, and grasped; by water—

The earth is overcome, swallowed, and seized; by the earth, food is overcome, swallowed, and seized; by food, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is overcome, swallowed, and seized; by the vital breath, the mind (*manas*) is overcome, swallowed, and seized;
by the mind, speech (*vāk*) is overcome, swallowed, and seized; by speech, the Vedas are overcome, swallowed, and seized; by the Vedas, the sacrifice (*yajña*).
"Overcome, swallowed, and seized"—these indeed are the twelve great elements established according to this rule;
among them, the sacrifice is the most excellent.

Those who know this thus think, "We know him," yet they do not know him as he truly is. This sacrifice is established in the Vedas; the Vedas are established in speech; speech is established in the mind;
the mind is established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the vital breath is established in food; food is established in the earth; the earth is established in water; and water is established in light.
Light is established in air; air is established in space; space is established in Brahman;

and Brahman is established in the Brāhmaṇa who knows Brahman. Verily, he who knows this is a knower of Brahman; he obtains holy fame and fragrant scents, and, with his evil dispelled, he enjoys infinite prosperity—he who knows thus.
And he who, knowing thus, worships this Upaniṣad— the perfection of the Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas— thus says the Brāhmaṇa.

"The waters, generating the embryo"—thus the person is the embryo of the waters; he is the sacrifice. When the sacrifice is being led forward by the waters, it breathes out toward the east; therefore, he causes water for sipping to be brought first. When he sips, he sips three times; he cleans his lips twice.
Having descended into life, he drives away evil. Having set it down, having lifted it with a *yajus*-formula, having employed the mantras, and having settled it, [he places] them facing eastward.

The branches have their origin in the junction; the thumb and the hand are his immortality, and the water is the under-layer for him. Saying, "I spread the under-layer for you, who are immortal," he pours water into the hand and sips it three times with the hymn beginning, "O living ones. When he sips first, he thereby causes the seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) that are outside the body to swell within him.
The measures are as follows: fire, wind, the sun, the moon, the waters, cattle, and other creatures;

he causes them to swell in him by means of this [second sip]. Water is immortality. When he drinks the second time, he causes the seven downward breaths (*apāna*) to swell in him—namely, those which are external to the body.
The portions are as follows: the full moon, the eighth-day rite, the new moon, faith, consecration, sacrifice, and the sacrificial fees;
by this [third sip], he causes them to swell in him—the waters, which are immortality.
When he sips for the third time, he causes the seven vyānas to swell in him, for these are the vital breaths that flow outward from the body.
The measures are as follows: this earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, the seasons, the seasonal periods, and the years;
he causes these to swell in him by means of this [offering]. Water, immortality, the person (puruṣa), and Brahman—thus there is an explanatory verse:
"Therefore, indeed, the wise one knows that this lotus is the person; he is the breath (prāṇa), for he lies within the city (puri śete); thus he is called 'he who lies within the city' (puriśaya)."
The breath (*prāṇa*), dwelling in the city [of the body], they call "the person" (*puruṣa*) by an indirect name;
for the gods, as it were, prefer the indirect and dislike the direct.
When he sips water first, he thereby secures for himself the fore-offerings (*purastāddhoma*) in this [body]. When he sips water a second time...

By that [first sipping], he secures for himself the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāgau*) in this [sacrifice]; when he sips a third time, by that he secures for himself the *saṃsthita-homas* (concluding oblations) in this [sacrifice]. When he twice wipes his mouth, that constitutes the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). When he causes all the cavities and the entire body to swell, and whatever else is the work of the mantra in the sacrifice that might be omitted, all that he secures for himself by this; when he employs the mantras preceded by "Oṃ."

Up to the Sarvamedha sacrifice, these are his rites; for him who knows this, there is freedom of movement and liberation at will in all worlds, among all gods, in all Vedas, among all beings, and among all creatures, and he does not perish even in the midst of life.
This is also stated in a Rigvedic verse:
The waters are the form of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; the waters consist of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
Every being consists of water; everything consists of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
Within these are the three Vedas, following after the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
"The flower of the waters, the embodiment, the sky, the supreme purifier"— having sipped water and sprinkled himself with this, he recites over himself the mantra "Indra jīva" (O Indra,
live!), according to the Brāhmaṇa.
The Second Chapter. "Oṃ! The Brahmacārī moves through both worlds," with these words he addresses the teacher.
"In him the gods become of one mind," with these words he addresses Vāyu. He goes instantly from the eastern ocean to the northern ocean.

Thus the consecrated one speaks to the sun: "This one with long hair is the consecrated one; this one with long hair stands in the place of the teacher and is praised as 'the teacher'; standing in the place of lightning he is praised as 'Vāyu'; standing in the place of heaven he is praised as 'Āditya'."
This is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse: "The student, eating... so says the Brāhmaṇa.
When a Brāhmaṇa is born, seven faculties are born with him: spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), fame, sleep, anger, boastfulness, beauty, and holy fragrance as the seventh.
These indeed approach him when he has entered upon the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*); his spiritual luster goes to the wild animals.
He sees his teacher as a python, sleep as a boar, anger as praise, a young girl as beauty, and the plants and trees as a holy fragrance.

When he wears deer-skins, by that he wins spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), which resides in deer; having bathed together with them, he becomes possessed of spiritual luster. As for the fact that he performs service for his teacher day after day—

By that, he secures for himself whatever glory belongs to his teacher; having bathed together, he becomes glorious. When, desiring to sleep, he pours out the water, by that he secures for himself that sleep which belongs to the python (*ajagara*). Of him who has thus bathed and is sleeping, they say: "He is sleeping; wake him up! Even when angry, he does not harm anyone with his speech, from person to person.
Thinking himself as one who is worse, he restrains that anger of his which arises toward the boar;

for when he has bathed, those [anger-possessing beings] enter him, who is more praiseworthy than anger. Therefore, one should not bathe while praising oneself with water, for by that he restrains the praise which belongs to the waters; having bathed together [with them], he becomes more praiseworthy than foods and more praiseworthy than [other] praises. Now, this is for the religious student (brahmacārin).

Regarding the form (*rūpa*) that belongs to the maiden, one should cause those naked ones to gaze upon it; thus one should have her face veiled. By this means, one secures that form which exists in the maiden.

When he has bathed, they gaze upon him as if upon a maiden. Now, there is a holy fragrance belonging to the herbs and trees; having cut off that holy fragrance of theirs, one should not smell it. By this [means], one secures it.
He who possesses that meritorious fragrance found in the herbs and trees becomes one who has bathed and is fragrant with merit.
Indeed, approaching in this manner, he approaches Agni with one quarter, his teacher with one quarter, the village with one quarter,
and Death with one quarter. When, having brought fuel every day, he attends upon the fire in the evening and in the morning,
by that he wins for himself that quarter which belongs to him in the fire.
In that he performs service for his teacher day after day, by that he wins that quarter of him which resides in the teacher.

In that, having entered the village day after day, he seeks only alms and not sexual intercourse, by that he wins that quarter of him which resides in the village. In that, even when angry, he does not harm anyone with his speech from person to person...
Thinking him to be evil, he seizes that very foot which belongs to him in the realm of death.
Indeed, five fires are established in the religious student (*brahmacārin*): two in his hands separately, one in his mouth, one in his heart, and the fifth in his lap.
When he does not touch a woman with his right hand, by that he wins the world of those who sacrifice day after day;

when [he does not touch her] with his left hand, by that [he wins the world] of those who have gone forth as wanderers (*pravrājin*); when [he does not touch her] with his mouth, by that [he wins the world] of those who leap into the fire (*agnipraskandin*); and when [he does not touch her] with his heart, by that [he wins the world] of heroes.
Whatever [merit] belongs to householders by means of their sexual organ, if he carries away a woman with those [organs], he remains as if without a fire.

When he daily attends upon the teacher in the family, having performed that service, he should say: "May Dharma protect me; may I guard Dharma. For Dharma, thus protected, will protect him. His offspring will become better and better day by day.

The *dhāyyā* verse is indeed placed [in its position]; it establishes the ancestors in the heavenly world. One should not wear woven cloth (*tāntava*). He who wears woven cloth increases the *kṣatra*, not the *brahman*; therefore, one should not wear woven cloth, thinking, "May the *brahman* increase, not the *kṣatra*. One should not sit above [another]. When one sits above, he makes his own vital breath inferior to that of the person below, just as the wind blows.

"He should sit below, lie down below, stand below, and walk below; for in this way, indeed, the ancient Brahmins used to practice the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). When his son or brother was suffering, they would say to him, 'Bring him here! until the time of fetching the firewood; while intending to chant the *svara* chants, he may eat food. Then they say regarding the rear part [of the body]: 'Bathe him! until the time of fetching the firewood."

For these are not [ordinary] vows. If the teacher addresses him while he is lying down, he should rise and respond. If [the teacher addresses him] while he is lying down, having risen; if [he addresses him] while he has stood up, having approached him; if [he addresses him] while he has approached, even as he is running toward him—thus indeed did the ancient Brahmins practice their studentship (*brahmacarya*). Such was their meritorious fame.
"He goes," or "He will go today," he says.
Janamejaya Pārīkṣita, while out on a hunt, approached two swans that were teaching [others] by saying, "Stay close!
They spoke to Janamejaya Pārīkṣita as he drew near; he said, "Homage to you both, O Blessed Ones! Who are you, O Blessed Ones?
They replied, "We are the Dakṣiṇāgni and the Āhavanīya fires. He said, "Homage to you both, O Blessed Ones!"
"Then, let us go," he said. "Even to a grove," they replied. "Indeed, even the gods do not find delight; for the gods do not find delight even in a single grove.

"And yet, the gods go from one grove to another," he said. He [the king] replied, "Homage to you two, O Blessed Ones! What is meritorious? "Celibacy (brahmacarya). "What is worldly? "Celibacy alone. "Who knows that? [He replied,] "Dantāvala."

Now, at that very time, Dhaumra Dantāvala approached Janamejaya Pārīkṣita. Rising up for him, he himself provided a seat. Having greeted him, [Janamejaya] asked: "Sir, what is meritorious? "Vedic studentship (brahmacarya). "What is worldly? "Vedic studentship alone. He then taught this to him: the forty-eight [year vow].

A year of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*) for each Veda; having thus divided it fourfold among the Vedas, one should practice twelve years of *brahmacarya*. One may also perform it for at least twelve years, or even longer according to one's ability. To him [who has completed this], he gave a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh—this is also what is proclaimed. Some say that the teacher is a *brahmacārī*; [he is] space as the deity above, and then, with respect to the self, he is a Brāhmaṇa who possesses vows and possesses conduct.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī).

Brahman indeed delivered all creatures to Death; however, he did not deliver the religious student (*brahmacārin*). He said, "In this [world], in this [person]?"—"What is it?"—"Whatever night he should spend without having brought firewood, by that much he shall be deprived of his life-span. Therefore, a religious student, having brought firewood day after day, should attend upon the fire morning and evening; he should not place it on top [of the fire].
Now, if one should establish [the fire] and place [the oblation] upon it, that day Parjanya rains like a cloud.

Those gods said, "This is indeed a Brahmin who will practice the life of a student; tell him, 'Ask for alms! [They replied,] "Tell him, 'From the householder! [And they asked,] 'What shall she withhold from him who gives? [The answer was: 'His merit from sacrifices and charitable works, and his wealth.'"

"He shall obtain it"—therefore, one should give alms daily to the religious student (*brahmacārin*); they should approach the housewife [with this thought]: "May he obtain the merit of his sacrifices and charitable works, as well as his wealth.

He must not let the seventh night pass; for by letting the seventh night pass, he ceases to be a religious student. Having failed to attend to the sacred fuel and to beg for alms for seven nights, the religious student must be initiated again.
He should not sleep on high [beds], nor sing, nor dance, nor run, nor spit. If he sleeps on high...
Frequent dwellings arise because he becomes a singer; they run to the cries of lamentation because he becomes a dancer;
they carry out the deceased because he becomes a reciter; the subjects go to sleep because he becomes a storyteller.
As for what he spits, he spits that upon his own middle. If he should spit, [he should say]: "From heaven indeed [I spit] me; whatever is here also [is spat]."
"Of the honey, may I have that which is here; may it be mine"—with these words he consecrates himself.
"Whatever of the honey is here, which has been offered, spilled, or forgotten—may Agni and Savitṛ place that back within my belly."
"That essence of mine which has flown away elsewhere—let us summon it back here; may it swell within me again.

He should not stand upon a cremation ground; if he should stand there, he should take water in his hand and consecrate it with the mantra: "If this [essence] has departed through desire for the seasons..."

While reciting, "If we have approached this sin of desire during the season, like a blind man or a cripple, let it perish; let not the sin that comes after us reach us," he should sprinkle himself and circumambulate, proceeding toward the Samayā.
Now, this student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) is indeed consecrated by the gods (*pariṣūta*);
concerning this, it is also said in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"This consecration of the gods moves about, shining and unassailed; in it are all cattle, in it are the sacrifices, in it is food together with the deities"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"Generating the out-breath and the in-breath," so saying, at the base of the conch, the son of the great seer Vasiṣṭha uttered these words: "Let cold and heat appear here as two springs. And so it has continued forever. Now, indeed, in the middle of Vipāś is the first hermitage called Vasiṣṭhaśilā, and the second is Kṛṣṇaśilā; there Vasiṣṭha performed his penance.

Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni perform penance at Jāmadagna; Gautama and Bharadvāja, as lions, perform penance at Prabhasa; Guṅgu performs penance at Guguvāsa; the seer performs penance at Ṛṣidroṇa; Agastya performs penance at Agastyatīrtha; Atri performs penance in Divya;
Svayambhū Kaśyapa performed penance on the Kaśyapatuṅga peak; and the wolf, the bear, the hyena, and the dog [perform penance] there.

The Varāha, Cilvaṭi, and Babhruka serpents, having their fangs removed and their jaws joined together by Kaśyapa upon his lofty vision, attained perfection from the Saraṇavāṭa [hermitage]. As a celibate student in the forest of the seers, he stood on one foot for a thousand divine years;
for a second thousand years, he held a stream of nectar upon his head for forty-eight thousand divine years.
On the surface of the water, Śiva performed austerity; from that austerity which had been performed, he performed yet further austerity.
Regarding this, these *ṛc* verses speak: "Generating out-breath and in-breath," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"One-footed, two-footed"—Vāyu is one-footed; space is his foot. The moon is two-footed; its two halves, the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, are its feet.

The sun is three-footed; these worlds are its feet. Fire is six-footed; earth, the intermediate space, heaven, the waters, the plants, and the trees—these beings are its feet. For all of them, the Vedas are the goal, and they are established in the Self.

There are four branches of the Brahman; moreover, they say there are six: form and space. By means of the *ṛc*, form [is established]; the movement is that of the *yajus*; the splendor consists of the *sāman*; and this is the water of the *Bhṛgvaṅgirases*. This very Brahman is the sacrifice, four-footed and twice established. Of that, the *Bhṛgvaṅgirases* are the two establishments; moreover, they say it is "once established" because the Hotṛ performs the circles of the *ṛcs*. Through these, he causes the earth to swell, for in her Agni moves.
This is also stated in a Rigvedic verse:
"O Earth, you are clothed in fire, you are the thunder.
When the Adhvaryu performs an action with a Yajus formula, he thereby causes the intermediate space to swell; in that [space], Vāyu does not settle, nor does he utter any [specific] portion of it.
This has also been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:

"Moving along the paths in the intermediate space, it does not settle on any day whatsoever. The first-born source of the waters and of cosmic order (ṛta)—where was he born, and from whence did he come into being?"
That which the Udgātṛ performs with the Sāman, by that he causes the sky to swell; for there the bright Āditya moves.
This has also been stated in a Ṛc:
"The high-flying, ruddy bird."
When one performs the *brahmārca* with the *kāṇḍas*, one thereby causes the waters to swell, for the moon moves within the waters.
This is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"The moon is within the waters."

From them come the herbs and trees; from them, by means of their roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, sprouts, juices, and scents, the sacrifice proceeds. By water ritual acts proceed; by water Soma is pressed. Therefore, when one addresses the Brahman priest at every ritual act, one thereby gives permission with water; for this is his portion. It is just as when one who is about to eat [first takes] water.
In this way one should first cause [the sacrificer] to sip water; afterwards, in this same manner, the sacrifice proceeds by means of water and is concluded in water.

Therefore, the Brahman priest causes the sacrifice to proceed through the *purastāddhoma* and *saṃsthita-homa* offerings. For by means of the *purastāddhoma* and *saṃsthita-homa* offerings, he encompasses the sacrifice within himself. For it is by encompassing the sacrifice within himself that the *Bhṛgus* and *Aṅgirases*, having milked out the Vedas, consider themselves drinkers of Soma.
For this Veda has Soma as its essence;
this is also stated in a Rigvedic verse: "He thinks he has drunk Soma."

Thus: just as one quiets the rain with this earth when it is stirred up, smoking with light, even so does Brahmā quiet the injury of the sacrifice by means of the *vyāhṛtis* of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases. "Agni for me unto Āditya"—these are the Aṅgirases; these indeed pervade all this. "Vāyu, the waters, the moon"—these are the Bhṛgus; these [pervade] this...
"Having completed everything, they cause it to swell; it becomes a single entity," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

There was indeed a man named Vicārī Kābandhi, the son of Kabandha Ātharvaṇa; he was wise, a seeker of truth, and well-versed in the sacred scriptures. Yet, due to his own excessive pride, he did not seek human wealth. His mother said to him: "Those very people have declared this food for you—among these Kurus, Pañcālas, Aṅgas, Magadhas, Kāśis, Kosalas, Śālvas, Matsyas, Śivasas, Uśīnaras, and the northerners."

"They eat food," he said; "but because of your excessive pride, we have become unable to eat, O child. Seek a vehicle! He then came to King Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, the sovereign ruler of the whole earth, at the time when the Soma had been pressed.
Having entered the sacrificial hall, he addressed the officiating priests and the sacrificer: "Those rivers which flow toward the east, those which flow toward the south, and those..."

Those that flow westward and those that flow northward—all these are called by distinct names; yet when they reach the ocean, their individual names are cut away, and they are simply called "the ocean. In the same way, all these Vedas have been produced, together with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), the explanatory treatises (*brāhmaṇa*), the esoteric teachings (*upaniṣad*), the histories (*itihāsa*), the narrative legends (*anvākhyāta*), the ancient lore (*purāṇa*), and the phonetic accents (*svara*).
Accompanied by ritual formulations, etymologies, instructions, refinements, and dialogues, when they undertake the sacrifice, their designation "sacrifice" is cut off;
they call it simply "yajña."

Indeed, that ground which is not sloping toward the east, nor sloping toward the north, which is artificial, or which is uneven—that is a site for sacrifice cut off from the gods. But this indeed is a site for sacrifice: that which is level, well-rooted, unburnt, firmly established, sloping toward the northeast, even, and as if strewn with grass—wherein there is the Brahminhood of a Brahmin.

"Let us know: 'Does Brahmā perform the office of Brahmā?'—thus you spoke regarding the Veda; yet we do not find that by which we may proceed further. He then questioned them: "What does the Hotṛ priest know when he performs the duties of the Hotṛ? What does the Adhvaryu know when he performs the duties of the Adhvaryu?
What does the Udgātṛ know when he performs the duties of the Udgātṛ? What does the Brahmā know when he performs the office of Brahmā?"—thus he spoke.

"We do not find that desire by which we might go further," they said. We reply: Speech itself is the Hotṛ; it performs the office of the Hotṛ, for through speech the hymns and the *vaṣaṭ*-cries are accomplished. We say: Speech itself is the Hotṛ; Speech is the Brahman; Speech is the deity.

Through out-breath and in-breath the Adhvaryu performs the office of the Adhvaryu; out-breath is the *praṇītā* waters, for all beings are led forth (*praṇīta*) by out-breath; out-breath is the *praṇītā*. We say: Out-breath and in-breath themselves are the two Adhvaryus; out-breath and in-breath...

"Brahman is the out-breath and the in-breath; the deity. With the eye alone the Udgātṛ performs the office of the Udgātṛ, for with the eye these beings see; moreover, the eye is the Udgātṛ, the eye is Brahman, the eye is the deity. With the mind alone the Brahman priest performs the office of the Brahman, for with the mind one perceives what is horizontal, what is upward, and whatever else there is—all that he performs with the mind alone is Brahman. We declare this to you: the mind is indeed the Brahman priest. The mind is Brahman. The mind is the deity. Thus, O Gārgya, you have not known Brahman.
