"Brahman is the mind, the god," so [it is said].

For example, if the sacrificer and the officiating priests were here to call heaven "earth" and earth "heaven," no one else would approve of that; likewise, he does not approve of this [misidentification] if one were to speak thus. But how then should one speak? One should call the Hotṛ priest "Hotṛ," speech "Speech," the Brahman "Brahman," and the deity "Deity."

One should address the Adhvaryu as "Adhvaryu," as "out-breath and in-breath," and as "Brahman"; one should address the deity as "deity. One should address the Udgātṛ as "Udgātṛ," as "the eye," as "Brahman," and as "deity.
One should address the Brahman-priest as "Brahman," as "mind," as "Brahman," and as "deity. (GopBr 1.2.12)

Indeed, these various doctrines arise among living beings: those who cause one who has drunk *asoma* to sacrifice, those who cause one who has drunk *surā* to sacrifice, and those who cause a Brāhmaṇa who has discontinued the *soma*-sacrifice to sacrifice. In the morning, they should approach him with fuel in their hands, saying, "We come to you, sir.
[He asks: "For what purpose? [They reply: "Those very questions which your honor asked us, which your honor [asked]..."

"Explain them," he said; "So be it," they replied, and he explained these questions to them: "That by which one lays hold of both what exists here and what does not exist—that is Brahman. He who knows that is a Brāhmaṇa. One who studies and, having studied, explains [it]—thus they call him a Brāhmaṇa.
This is the Brāhmaṇa.

Now, therefore, concerning the places of sacrifice (*devayajana*): the self is a place of sacrifice; faith is a place of sacrifice; the officiating priests are a place of sacrifice; the earth is a place of sacrifice. Now, that which is the place of sacrifice consisting of the self is this very body which one inhabits, whether one is performing religious duties or not. This is the sacrifice; this one sacrifices; they sacrifice to this; this is the place of sacrifice. And furthermore—
Faith is the place of sacrifice; whenever one should take it up, faith indeed does not pass him by—that is a place of sacrifice.
Furthermore, this is a place of sacrifice belonging to the officiating priests: wherever a learned Brāhmaṇa performs [the rite] with a mantra, that is a place of sacrifice.
Furthermore, this is a place of sacrifice belonging to the earth: wherever waters stand, wherever they flow, and where they carry away and bring forth [the soil], that is a place of sacrifice.

That is a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) which is level, with its roots intact, undisturbed by fire, and well-established; it slopes toward the east and north, is even as if strewn with grass, and from which there is no pit, ant-hill, tree, mountain, river, or path in front. One should not leave a space the size of a sacrificial ground in front, nor should they sit down to the north of the fire.
The Brāhmaṇa section. GpBr 1.2.14.

Aditi, desiring offspring, cooked rice-porridge; she ate the remnant of it and conceived a fetus, from which the Ādityas were born. This rice-porridge that is being cooked serves as a support and as a foothold. The fuel-sticks are a span long, for the self is thus measured by Prajāpati. Indeed, that body of Agni which is fit for sacrifice is in the *aśvattha* tree.

He unites with her through this self-sustaining body, namely the clarified butter; when he anoints the fuel-sticks with clarified butter, he causes him to prosper through those two bodies. When he places the *nirmārga* grass upon them, it is because power is produced through concealment (*avakūti*); in that he places the *nirmārga*, it is indeed through concealment. The year is procreation, and Agni is procreation; this is [the means of] procreation.
The year is procreation; when he places a kindling-stick on the fire with a *ṛc*-verse, the progenitor thereby causes him to be born from procreation.

Man indeed protects [him], for man does not know that which he is born to eat; he attains that constellation which is this rice-porridge being cooked. When the kindling-sticks are placed, it is the womb itself that is thus prepared for the seed.

That is sustained: the year is indeed seed when deposited; he who establishes the fire after the year has passed establishes it for Prajāpati himself. [One should establish it] twelve nights before the year [is completed], for those are the image of the year; or on three nights, or on two, or on the day before the establishment. These, indeed, are the Ādityas for one establishing the fire.

"Or else, from here onwards, may these [gods] protect my income in that world on the path; thus they ward off one who intends to sacrifice. For the Ādityas are indeed the sharers of the remnants—whatever is left over. When he anoints the fuel-sticks with what is left over, he announces it to them alone; having announced it to them alone, they go to the heavenly world.
Prajāpati, the divine Atharvan, having performed austerity, fashioned this *brahmaudana* to be consumed by four persons;

it consists of four worlds, four deities, four Vedas, and four officiating priests (*hautra*). Indeed, these worlds are four: earth, the intermediate space, heaven, and the waters. These deities are four: Agni, Vāyu, Āditya, and Candramas. These Vedas are four.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Brahmaveda— these are the four *hotrās*, namely the office of the *hotṛ*, the *adhvaryu*, the *udgātṛ*, and the *brahman*.
This is also stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, seven are his hands;
bound in three places, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals.
Regarding this, "four are his horns" refers to the Vedas; "three are his feet" refers to the *savana*s (the three daily soma-pressings); and "two are his heads" refers to... [the two worlds].

The *brahmaudana* and the *pravargya* rites are indeed [the subject]; "seven are his hands" refers to the *chandases*; "bound in three ways" is the mantra, the ritual rule (*kalpa*), and the explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*).

"The bull bellows"—this one is indeed the bull; he bellows when he recites the *śastras* at the sacrifices with *ṛcs*, *yajus* formulas, *sāmans*, and *brahman* hymns. "The great god has entered into mortals."
This indeed is the great deity that the sacrifice entered among mortals.
"He who would know the seven downward paths," he says, referring to the out-breaths (*prāṇas*). "He who would know the seven distant paths," he says, referring to the in-breaths (*apānas*).
"He who would know the head of the sacrifice"—this indeed is the head of the sacrifice, namely the *brahmaudana* accompanied by mantras. He who...
"If one were to approach this *brahmaudana* without it being accompanied by mantras, he would indeed have approached the sacrifice headless.
Therefore, one should approach only the *brahmaudana* that is accompanied by mantras, not that which is without mantras"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Why is Ātreya the one who knows the secondary sacrifice (*upayajña*)? Because darkness had seized the Sun, Atri dispelled it; that Atri perceived.
This has also been stated in a *ṛc*:
"Atri brought the heaven upward from the beginning of praise; having become celestial, Atri established the Sun for the sake of making [the world] visible."

He said to him, "Choose a boon. He replied, "May my offspring be worthy of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇīya). Therefore, the first sacrificial gift at a sacrifice is given to one of the Atri lineage; so says the Brāhmaṇa. Prajāpati spoke to the Vedas, saying, "Lay the fires. Speech addressed them, saying, "The horse is indeed the best of all materials. They brought it forth from the terrible, cruel lake of water. Speech addressed them, saying, "Let the horse be appeased. "So be it," they said.
The Ṛgveda approached him and said, "I shall pacify the horse. He released a great terror against it as it had not yet departed;
it took refuge in this eastern direction. He said, "This horse is still unpacified.

The Yajurveda approached him and said, "I shall pacify the horse. He released a great terror against it as it had not yet departed; it took refuge in this western direction. He said, "This horse is still unpacified."

The Sāmaveda approached him and said, "I shall pacify the horse. [He asked,] "But with what will you pacify it? [It replied,] "My Sāman named Rathantara is neither terrible nor cruel; by it the horse is praised. Then, as that [horse] was being released, he created that very same great terror. It took refuge in this northern direction. He said, "This horse is indeed not yet pacified."

Speech said to them, "Go to Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa. Having approached Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa as he sat there, they said, "Homage be to you, O Blessed One; may the horse be healed. "So be it," he replied. He then addressed the son of Kabandha Ātharvaṇa, saying, "O Discerning One! "Blessed One," he responded to him, and promised, "The horse shall be healed. "So be it," he said. Then the descendant of Atharvan prepared the water for pacification (*śāntyudaka*).

He pacifies [the horse] with the *cāṅgirasa*, the *ābhiśvatanas*, the *mātṛnāman*, and the *vāstoṣpati* hymns. When that horse has been bathed and sprinkled, embers fell from every single hairy pore of its body. The horse, being satisfied, offered a salutation: "Homage to Śaṃyu Ātharvaṇa, who caused me to perform the sacrifice. Indeed, there will be other Brāhmaṇas after this one.

"Those who possess the most abundant equipment will place [the fire] upon the footprint of the sun—either that of an ox, a calf, a goat, a *śravaṇa* bird, or a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*). For this earth is indeed the footprint of the sun; thus it will be placed upon its own footprint. While the fire is being led forward and the horse is being touched from behind, the Brahman makes the sacrificer recite these five verses beginning with, "When you first cried out at birth..."
The Brahmins escort him; he thus commences the Brahma-rite. "He who knows the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases is indeed a learned, all-knowing Brahmā"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

The gods and the Asuras were contending with one another. Those gods said to Indra, "Guard this sacrifice of ours until we have joined battle with the Asuras. He replied, "Guard it for us in that form by which you mostly conceal yourself, so that you will be able to protect it. Having become the Ṛgveda, he stood waiting, having gone around and stationed himself in front.

The gods said, "Assume another form; with this form you do not cover us most extensively, nor will you be able to protect us. Having become the Yajurveda, he went around to the west and stood there. The gods said to him, "Assume another form; with this form you do not cover us most extensively, nor will you be able to protect us."

Thus, having become the Sāmaveda, he went around to the north and stood there. The gods said to him, "Assume another form indeed; with this form you do not cover us most effectively; with this you will not be able to protect us.
Then Indra, wearing a turban and having become the Brahmaveda, went around to the south and stood there. The gods said to him: "This..."
"Assume that form; with this form you will conceal yourself most effectively, and with it you will be able to protect us.
When Indra, having become the *brahmavedas* (the Brahman-knowing one) wearing a turban (*uṣṇīṣin*), went around to the south and stood there, he became the *brahman*.
That is the *brahmatva* (the state of being the *brahman*) of the *brahman*. This very thing is the form of Atharvan: the *brahman* wearing a turban. To his south stood the Viśvedevas.
When the Viśvedevas sat to his south, he became the Sadasya; that is the reason for the Sadasya’s name as Sadasya.
Indeed, strength is produced from this very strength when there is a Sadasya. For they find a much larger pen for a flock that is diseased.
This southern quarter is indeed terrible, while the others are peaceful; therefore, the Brahman priest recites the consecratory formulas over those [verses] that have been chanted.
"By mind alone the Sadasya produces them," he says; by muttering this *vyāhṛti* and by reflecting, he generates himself and establishes himself in victory.
The gods said to him, "Choose a boon. "I choose," he replied. He chose this boon:
"May they stand in this very office of the Hotṛ, purifying me, praising me, and reciting for me while I have become Indra. Thus, in that very office...

While purifying, praising, and reciting, they stood at the *hotrā* where Indra had become present. Because they stood at that very *hotrā*, purifying, praising, and reciting while Indra was present, he became the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī*. That is why the office of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* is called *brāhmaṇācchaṃsitva*. This *hotrā* of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* is indeed the one belonging to Indra.

"Choose a second boon," said Chaṃsīya. "I choose it," he replied. "In this very office of the Hotṛ, may they stand purifying, praising, and reciting me while I have become Vāyu. So, in that very office of the Hotṛ, they stood purifying, praising, and reciting him as he had become Vāyu.
Because they stood purifying, praising, and [reciting] him in that very office of the Hotṛ while he had become Vāyu...

Praising, standing, he became that; that is the office of the Potṛ. This very Hotrā belonging to Vāyu is the office of the Potṛ. "Choose a third boon," [Indra said]. "I choose," he replied. He chose this boon: "In this very office of the Hotṛ, may they stand kindling me as Agni, purifying me, praising me, and reciting for me. Thus, in that very office of the Hotṛ, he was kindled as Agni.

Kindling, purifying, praising, and reciting, they stood by him. Because they stood by him while kindling, purifying, praising, and reciting as he had become Agni within that very office of the Hotṛ, that became the Āgnīdhra; that is the reason for the Āgnīdhra’s name as Āgnīdhra. "This office of the Āgnīdhra is the Hotṛ-function belonging to Agni," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin indeed bore this Agni Vaiśvānara.
This very Agni Vaiśvānara, being borne by the Brahmin, generates these worlds; then this Agni Jātavedas looks out. Indeed, this Agni Vaiśvānara blazes with the Brahmin as his companion; come now, I—
"Whatever splendor, faculty, and vigor there is in me, let me display that, lest they consume me. Thus he nourished himself;
he milked it as milk and, having shown this [milk] to the Brahmin, offered it into himself. He nourished himself a second time;
he milked it as ghee and, having shown this [ghee] to the Brahmin, offered it into himself. He nourished himself a third time.
Having shown this entire transformed food to this Brāhmaṇa, he offered it into himself;

he thereby nourished his fourth self. With that, he beheld the Virāj, the wife of the Brāhmaṇa, and gave her to him. That self became his own. Then, the Brāhmaṇa who was about to cast away this Agni Vaiśvānara [beheld] Agni Jātavedas.

He placed it down and said, "O Agni Jātavedas, place this within me. He gave him two names: Aghora and Akrūra. He became a horse; therefore, a horse draws a chariot, but he does not carry a rider on his back.
He went to the gods and stood behind the gods; therefore, the gods were afraid of him. They gave him to Brahmā.
He appeased it with this ṛc-verse.
"They say that Agni Vaiśvānara has entered the cattle, burning away from his dwellings.
Do you, O God, speak for us among the gods so that we may not suffer harm at your hands.
With these five verses beginning with "When you first cried out as you were being born," he initiates him [Agni].

He became still; therefore, the horse among animals is not hungry, for he is Vaiśvānara. Therefore, one gives a horse as a fee to the Brahman priest, for it was given to the Brahman. He pressed out its essence, and that became the *rasa*.
This is indeed *rasa*, yet they call it "chariot" (*ratha*) cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic.
For the gods become as if invisible to those who do not see them face-to-face.

He went to the gods and stood behind the gods; therefore the gods were afraid of him. They gave him to the Brahman, and he offered him with this verse and an oblation of clarified butter: "The vigor of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts."
Having mounted the chariot, he stood upon it with this verse: "O Lord of the Forest, may you be strong-limbed!

Therefore, one gives the chariot used for the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnīdhreya*) to the Brahman priest, for it was given to the Brahman; from that, the carpenter fashioned the *tanūjyeṣṭhā* as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
He beheld it in five forms: in the *ṛc*, in the *yajus*, in the *sāman*, in the peaceful, and in the terrible.

Of these, he gave two to the Brahman: speech and light. Speech, indeed, is the cow; light is gold. Therefore, at the establishment of the sacred fires (*āgnīdhreya*), one gives a cow to be consumed by four persons to the Brahman; for she was given to the Brahman. When the animals are being slaughtered, they cause [the sacrificer] to lose his sight. He thus places sight within himself. That which is sight is indeed gold; therefore, [he gives] the gold belonging to the establishment of the sacred fires.

He gives gold to the Brahman; for what is given to the Brahman, he places within his own self and thereby kindles it. That which he did not place within himself became glowing embers (āglā). Having become glowing embers, she entered the ocean. She burned the ocean;
therefore the ocean is difficult to traverse, for it was indeed burnt by Vaiśvānara. She rose up upon the earth; she burned the earth.
She went to the gods; she harmed the gods. Those gods ran to Brahmā. He neither sang nor danced.
This is that [sage] named Āglaiṣā Kāruvidā. Although he was Āglāhata, they call him Āglāgṛdha cryptically; for the gods, as it were, prefer the cryptic and dislike the manifest.

That Brāhmaṇa who is a singer or a dancer, they call him an *āglāgṛdha*; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should neither sing nor dance, lest he become an *āglāgṛdha*. Therefore, the oblation for Brahman comes first, and that for Prajāpati comes after; after the oblation for Prajāpati, the one for Brahman alone is supreme—thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Now, the Atharvans and the Āṅgirases beheld that Brahman through the eyes of Bhṛgu, yet they did not know it, thinking, "We indeed are all this, namely the Bhṛgus and the Āṅgirases."

Those gods offered the oblation belonging to Brahman into the Sāṃtapana fire; for this indeed is the oblation belonging to Brahman that is offered into the Sāṃtapana fire. This Brahmin is indeed the Sāṃtapana fire; from his vigor the gods took vigor, the ancestors [took] the *svadhā* with good intent, the Brahmins [attained] the heavenly world through faith, and the seers press the soma thereby.

In the end, the women kept [the sacrificial food] solely for themselves; the outsiders press [the Soma] with both [hands]. For if no oblation belonging to Brahman were set out at the sacrifice, men would be born from the oblations to Prajāpati as crooked beings. "He hears of those worlds," [says the text];
for he who offers the Agnihotra is indeed the father of the Āhavanīya, the Gārhapatya, and the Dakṣiṇāgni fires. Or rather, it is said: "He who offers the Agnihotra."
They rejoice in their own dear abode; for them, this Agni becomes preeminent as Sāṃtapana.
When his speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied; when his breath is satisfied, Vāyu is satisfied; when his eye is satisfied, Āditya is satisfied;
when his mind is satisfied, Candramas is satisfied; when his ear is satisfied, the quarters and the intermediate directions are satisfied; and when his fluids are satisfied, the waters are satisfied.
"When the body hairs are satisfied, the herbs and trees are satisfied; when the body is satisfied, the earth is satisfied.
Thus this Agni Sāṃtapana, being the best, being satisfied, satisfies them all"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"This oblation is for the Sāṃtapana [fire]"—for that Brahmin is indeed the Sāṃtapana fire whose *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *niṣkramaṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *godāna*, *cūḍākaraṇa*, *upanayana*, *āplavana*, *agnihotra*, *vratacaryā*, and other rites have been performed; he is the Sāṃtapana. But as for this one who is without the sacred fires (*anagnika*), he is like a clod of earth thrown into a jar. Just as a clod of earth thrown into a jar [is destroyed], so is he.
It is not fit for the purpose of purification, nor does it produce grain; even so is this Brāhmaṇa who maintains no sacred fire.

For that Brāhmaṇa who maintains no fire, there should be no offering to the gods (daiva) and no offering to the ancestors (pitrya); nor do his blessings from Vedic study or his blessings from sacrifice lead to heaven.
This very thing has also been stated in a Ṛgvedic verse:
"We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker, the all-knowing,
the one of good wisdom for this sacrifice"— so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Then Prajāpati, intending to sacrifice with Soma, said to the Vedas: "Whom among you shall I choose as the Hotṛ, whom as the Adhvaryu, whom as the Udgātṛ, and whom as the Brahman?
They replied: "Choose one who knows the Ṛgveda as the Hotṛ, one who knows the Yajurveda as the Adhvaryu, one who knows the Sāmaveda as the Udgātṛ, and one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasa as the Brahman.
For in this way, his sacrifice will be established in the four worlds, among the four classes of gods, in the four Vedas, and in the four [directions]."

In the *hotrā* offices, the four-footed sacrifice is established; he who knows this becomes firmly established through offspring and cattle. Therefore, choose one who knows the *Ṛgveda* as the *hotṛ*, for he knows the duties of the *hotṛ*. Agni is indeed the *hotṛ*; the earth is the abode of the *ṛcs*, Agni is the deity, and the *gāyatrī* is the metre. "Bhūḥ" is the *śukra*; therefore, choose him alone as the *hotṛ*—thus it is said of him.

For the conquest of this world, for the victory over this world, for the complete mastery of this world, for the attainment of this world, for the increase of this world, for the prosperity of this world, for the exaltation of this world, for the pervasion of this world,
for the sufficiency of this world, and for the fulfillment of this world; yet, if one does not know it thus...
They choose the Hotṛ first; thus their sacrifice is made redundant.

Choose one who knows the Yajus as the Adhvaryu, for he knows the office of the Adhvaryu. Vāyu indeed is the Adhvaryu; the atmosphere is the abode of the Yajus formulas, Vāyu is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the metre. "Bhuvaḥ" is the Śukra cup; therefore, choose him.
"Choose such a one as Adhvaryu," he said, "for this world. Now, if they choose an Adhvaryu who does not know this, their sacrifice is left deficient from behind.
Choose an Udgātṛ who knows the Sāman, for he knows the office of the Udgātṛ; the Sun indeed is the Udgātṛ, and the Sky is the Sāmans.
"The sun is the sphere, the deity; the Jagatī is the metre; 'Svar' is the Śukra. Therefore, choose him as the Udgātṛ.

"Of this world," he said, "and thus [it is]. Now, if they do not choose an Udgātṛ who knows this, their sacrifice is left deficient in the latter part. Choose one who knows the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ as the Brahman priest, for he knows the office of the Brahman; the moon, indeed, is the Brahman.
The waters are indeed the abode of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; the moon is their deity; the lightning is their [deity]; the Uṣṇih and Kakubh are their meters;
"Oṃ" is for the Atharvans; "Śukraṃ janat" is for the Aṅgirases. Therefore, choose him alone as your Brahman priest, for the conquest of this world, for the victory over this world, for this [world].
For the conquest of this world, for the attainment of this world, for the increase of this world, for the prosperity of this world, for the elevation of this world, for the pervasion of this world,
for the sufficiency of this world, and for the completion of this world; yet, if they do not choose such a knower as Brahman-priest, then [the failure] belongs to them on the right side alone.
The sacrifice is left deficient;
indeed,
their sacrifice is left deficient from the south.

The Third Prapāṭhaka. Om. The earth slopes toward the south; from the south, the waters flow. Therefore, the sacrificial grounds are as if higher than that [general] ground. Wherever the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases have their dwellings, it is just as the waters carry these worlds along. Thus...

Just as the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases carry all the gods, even so this sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) carries all the Vedas: "Oṃ" for the Ṛg-verses, "Oṃ" for the Yajus-formulas, "Oṃ" for the Sāman-chants, and "Oṃ" is the greeting for everything. Those who know this perform it as the final act at the sacrifice, saying: "O Gods, O Brahmans, come! Come!"—for these indeed are the gods.

The Brahmins think that those who are the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases are being praised, chosen, and summoned; no one other than a knower of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases should come to the sacrifice when chosen, for he attains the splendor of the sacrifice through his own splendor, and vigor through his own vigor, and glory through his own glory.
No one other than a knower of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases should come to the sacrifice unchosen, lest he should rob the sacrifice. Thus it is according to the former [rule].

Just as a calf, having drunk from its mother, must suckle her, so too should a Brahmin who knows the *Bhṛgu* and *Aṅgiras* hymns, being chosen, come to the sacrifice so that he does not rob the sacrifice.

For what would it carry, and what would it attain, if it were like a cow, or a horse, or a mule, or one-footed, two-footed, or three-footed? Therefore, choose only one who knows the *Ṛgveda* as the *Hotṛ*, and one who knows the *Yajurveda* as the *Adhvaryu*.

One who knows the *Sāman* should be the *udgātṛ*, and one who knows the *Atharva-Aṅgiras* should be the *brahman*. Thus, for such a person, the sacrifice is established in the four worlds, among the four gods, in the four Vedas, and in the four *hotrā*s; the four-footed sacrifice stands firm.

He who knows this, as well as he who knows the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and he who knows that which is to be sacrificed (*yajanīya*) in the sacrifice, [attains success] through offspring and cattle.
One who experiences [this] is a Brāhmaṇa. // GpBr 1.3.1 //

Prajāpati performed the sacrifice. He performed the office of the Hotṛ by means of the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu by means of the Yajurveda, the office of the Udgātṛ by means of the Sāmaveda, and the office of the Brahman by means of the Atharvāṅgirases. Indeed, he performs this great rite when he performs the office of the Hotṛ by means of the Ṛgveda, the office of the Adhvaryu by means of the Yajurveda, the office of the Udgātṛ by means of the Sāmaveda, and the office of the Brahman by means of the Atharvāṅgirases. This [sacrifice] is indeed composed of the three Vedas.

One wing of the sacrifice is consecrated [by the officiants]; with the mind alone, the Brahman priest consecrates the other wing of the sacrifice. Now, he who blows here is indeed the sacrifice; his path is both mind and speech, for it is by means of both mind and speech that one carries out the sacrifice. Therefore, this is the mind and this is speech. If, while speaking, one should not know [the truth], one should know: "Half of this [sacrifice] is mine."

"It has slipped from within the sacrifice. Just as a one-legged man, when walking, or a one-wheeled chariot, when moving, comes to ruin, even so his sacrifice comes to ruin. Following the ruin of the sacrifice, the sacrificer comes to ruin;
following the ruin of the sacrificer, the officiating priests come to ruin; and following the ruin of the officiating priests, the sacrificial fees come to ruin.

"Following the failure of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās), the sacrificer fails with respect to his sons and cattle; following the failure of his sons and cattle, the sacrificer fails with respect to the heavenly world; following the failure of the heavenly world, the security and prosperity (yogakṣema) of that half of the world in which they sacrifice fails. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. (GopB 1.3.2)

Regarding this, Śvetaketu Āruṇeya once said: "Having seen a Brahman priest speaking, [I thought] 'Half of this sacrifice has slipped away from me. Therefore, the Brahman priest restrains his speech during the *bahiṣpavamāna*, then during the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* cups, then during those [verses] which they recite for the *pavamāna*, and then during the *stotras* and *śastras* up until the *vaṣaṭkāra*. If he should suffer a lapse regarding the *ṛc*..."

One should conclude with "Oṃ bhūr janat" and offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire if [the error] was in the Yajus; one should offer in the Dakṣiṇāgni fire with "Oṃ bhuvo janat" if it was in the Sāman; one should offer in the Āhavanīya fire with "Oṃ svar janat" if it was in the Ṛc; and if it was an unknown Brahmanical error, one should offer in the Āhavanīya fire itself with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar janat oṃ. This applies to the Vākovākya, the Ṛcs, the Yajus, and the Sāmans.

Then, by means of the essence of the Atharvāṅgirases and of the Vedas, whatever is injured in the sacrifice is joined together. As it has been said, "as with salt," so it is: just as a man who has both feet, or a chariot with both wheels, remains steady when moving, even so his sacrifice remains steady; following the steadiness of the sacrifice, the sacrificer remains steady; following the steadiness of the sacrificer, [his offspring] remains steady.

Following the non-failure of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) proceed without failure; following the non-failure of the sacrificial fees, the sacrificer proceeds without failure in his sons and cattle; following the non-failure of his sons and cattle, the sacrificer proceeds without failure in the heavenly world (*svarga-loka*); and following the non-failure of the heavenly world, the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of that half [of the world] proceeds without failure.
"He incurs failure in that half [of the sacrifice] in which they offer," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

"Therefore, when the sacrificial fees are being led forth for the Udgātṛ, they are led with the thought: 'He has sat upon the Udumbara post for me; he has uttered the *hiṅ* for me; he has chanted the *prastāva* for me; he has been in the water for me; he has invoked the *subrahmaṇyā* for me. And for the Adhvaryu, [they are led] with the thought: 'He has drawn the cups for me; he has performed the circumambulation for me; they have listened to me; he has brought them into harmony for me; he has sacrificed for me; he has recited the *śastra* for me; he has not omitted the *vaṣaṭ*-call for me. And for the Hotṛ, [they are led] with the thought: 'He has sat upon the Hotṛ's seat for me; he has sacrificed for me.'"

"May he have praised for me; may he have uttered the *vaṣaṭ* for me"—thus [he says] regarding the Hotṛ. "May he have prepared the sacrificial ground for my gods; may the Brahman have seated himself for me; may he have muttered the *brahmajapa* for me; may he have offered the preliminary oblations and the concluding oblations for me; may he have sacrificed for me; may he have praised for me; may he have uttered the *vaṣaṭ* for me"—thus regarding the Brahman. "May he have performed for me with the greatest *brahman*"—this indeed is the greatest.

That which is Brahman is the Bhrigus and Angirases; those who are Angirases are the essence (rasa); that which is the Atharvans is the remedy (bheṣaja); that which is the remedy is the immortal (amṛta); that which is the immortal is Brahman. Indeed, this [Brahman] receives half of the share of the former officiating priests (ṛtvij), while the others receive the other half as belonging to the Brahman-priest. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
The gods and the Asuras engaged in battle. Thereupon, these three *hotraka* priests fell into distress.

Indra plundered their *ucchānti* chants and gave them to the *hotṛ*: the *ājya* became that of the *hotṛ*, the *prauga* that of the *potṛ*, and the *vaiśvadeva* became that of the *hotṛ*; the *niṣkevalya* became that of the *neṣṭṛ*, and the *marutvatīya*—the *hotṛ*'s [portion].

The Āgnimāruta hymn belonged to the Hotṛ, and the Āgnimāruta to the Āgnīdhra; therefore, that which is the Āgnimāruta is recited as if with greater repetition, because these [priests]—the Hotṛ, the Potṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Āgnīdhra—seem to be competing in their recitation. When [the Hotṛ] was bewildered, he thought, "Let the Brahman wear this [garment]," for it was as if he were the most excellent of them. He lost half of those [verses]: the first *arhaṇa* and the first *pada*.
"He should leave this for the sacrificial fee and this as a remnant," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

Uddālaka Āruṇi, having been chosen by the people of the North, caused them to perform a sacrifice. A gold coin was fastened to him as he went, for he was afraid of being censured, thinking, "I shall give this to whichever learned Brāhmaṇa might censure me.
Now, a fear of Uddālaka had seized the Brāhmaṇas of the North, [thinking]: "Here comes this man from Kuru-Pañcāla, a Brāhmaṇa, the son of a Brāhmaṇa."

"He has been chosen for the higher office; who can restrain him? With what hero shall we contend against him? They followed him from the very point where he had set out. They said to Śaunaka Svaidāyana, "Svaidāyana, you are indeed the most learned in the Veda among us; with you as our hero, let us contend against him. They followed him from the very point where he had set out.
He held [the staff] in that manner, and they followed him accordingly. He addressed him, saying, "O Svaidāyana!
But he, being resentful toward him, replied to the one who had been summoned, "O son of Gautama! Indeed, the son of Gautama ran away while holding the staff upright.
